title: High fuel costs and softening demand squeeze regional and short-haul markets in June 2026
description:
The regional and low-cost aviation sectors faced mounting pressures in June 2026, as high jet fuel prices and a weakening in price-sensitive demand drove contractions across global domestic and short-haul networks.
The United States domestic market remained in contraction, dropping 1.2% YoY, while Australia's domestic traffic flatlined completely compared to the previous year.
African carriers recorded the strongest overall passenger traffic growth of any region in June, surging by 3.8% year-on-year.
This robust performance was largely fueled by a significant 6.7% increase in international traffic, marking the highest international growth rate globally.
However, airlines in the region aggressively expanded their overall capacity by 4.7%, which ultimately outpaced passenger demand.
text:
The regional and low-cost aviation sectors faced mounting pressures in June 2026, as high jet fuel prices and a weakening in price-sensitive demand drove contractions across global domestic and short-haul networks.

According to the latest Air Passenger Market Analysis from IATA, industry-wide domestic passenger traffic declined by 3.0% year-on-year in June, marking a third consecutive month of contraction for domestic markets globally.

Overall domestic capacity also fell by 2.4% YoY, reducing the passenger load factor (PLF) to 84.0%.

Rising costs and reduced services are heavily impacting price-sensitive travelers, a core demographic for low-cost carriers.

In China, the region’s largest domestic market, elevated fuel costs weakened price-sensitive demand and extended capacity reductions, contributing to a steep 5.2% YoY drop in domestic traffic.

Similar cost pressures were felt in India, where the domestic market contracted by 0.5% YoY largely in response to soaring fuel prices.

In Japan, domestic traffic fell by 3.8% amid a highly challenging operating environment that has been severely exacerbated by high jet fuel prices and a weak yen.

“Global demand for air travel was down 1.7% in June compared to 2025. This is largely due to domestic market declines in China, the US, and Japan, and weak but improving international demand for Middle East carriers. While Middle East performance improved, renewed tensions will not help the region’s recovery and the knock-on impact of rising fuel prices will continue to burden travelers with higher airfares," said Willie Walsh, IATA’s Director General.

To mitigate escalating operating costs, airlines are increasingly being forced to rationalise their short-haul networks.

This trend is particularly evident in the Asia Pacific region, where the short-haul international segment took a direct hit from capacity reductions linked to higher fuel expenses.

As a result, passenger traffic on short-haul flights within Asia contracted by 2.6% YoY in June, marking the corridor's first decline since the pandemic.

Airlines pulled back on intra-Asia capacity by 4.8%, which paradoxically helped push the corridor's PLF up 1.9% to 82.8%. Several major regional markets, including Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam, all recorded traffic declines on intra-Asia routes during the month.

The United States domestic market remained in contraction, dropping 1.2% YoY, while Australia's domestic traffic flatlined completely compared to the previous year.

However, the regional and short-haul picture was not uniformly bleak. Brazil emerged as a rare bright spot, standing as the only major domestic market worldwide to maintain growth in June with a modest 0.9% YoY increase in passenger traffic.

In stark contrast to the global downturn in domestic and intra-regional travel, the African market showcased notable resilience.

African carriers recorded the strongest overall passenger traffic growth of any region in June, surging by 3.8% year-on-year.

This robust performance was largely fueled by a significant 6.7% increase in international traffic, marking the highest international growth rate globally.

However, airlines in the region aggressively expanded their overall capacity by 4.7%, which ultimately outpaced passenger demand.

As a result, the region's overall passenger load factor (PLF) dropped by 0.6 percentage points to 73.9%, and despite the surge in demand, Africa continued to record the lowest international PLF (74.2%) among all global regions.

Short-haul international travel within Europe, the world’s largest international route corridor, showed ongoing resilience, posting a 2.3% YoY increase in traffic.

Looking ahead, IATA says regional operators may soon see an improvement. Following three consecutive months of year-on-year declines, global scheduled seat capacity is expected to return to growth, with a 1.3% increase projected for July and a 2.6% rise anticipated in August.

"People continue to travel, which is an important contributor to global economic growth. There is no doubt, however, that stabilizing the situation in the Middle East and normalizing oil supplies would improve prospects for airlines, economies, and societies the world over,” said Walsh.

title: The well-being business emergency – It's time to protect your people and your profits
description:
At a recent roundtable luncheon on how to create meaningful connections in business, the conversation among the well-known business leaders landed authentically on a common theme: the pain, suffering and frustration in just about every aspect of our society.
But for that to happen, business leaders must promote the prosperity and well-being of their employees, their customers and the people in the communities in which they operate.
As Howard Schultz, former CEO of Starbucks and a true trailblazer of people-centric business, once said, “Success is not sustainable if it is defined by profit alone.
We must also consider the well-being of our people and the communities we serve.” Those who do will change the world for the better and realize unprecedented success.
They are building systems — financial, physical, emotional, social and technological — that treat well-being, stability, ownership and AI empowerment as the architecture of performance itself.
text:
At a recent roundtable luncheon on how to create meaningful connections in business, the conversation among the well-known business leaders landed authentically on a common theme: the pain, suffering and frustration in just about every aspect of our society.

However, there was also an overwhelming consensus that this was an incredible opportunity to reinvigorate — or even reinvent — the dream we call America. Though they drew from very different viewpoints and experiences, they agreed that the business community can lead us to realizing that dream in a way we have never seen before — to realize a world of abundance for every single human in this nation and this world.

But for that to happen, business leaders must promote the prosperity and well-being of their employees, their customers and the people in the communities in which they operate. As Howard Schultz, former CEO of Starbucks and a true trailblazer of people-centric business, once said, “Success is not sustainable if it is defined by profit alone. We must also consider the well-being of our people and the communities we serve.”

Those who do will change the world for the better and realize unprecedented success.

America is hurting – and people know it

Sadly, in the wake of the United States’ 250th anniversary, a December 2025 Pew Research Center survey of 3,560 US adults found that most Americans say the country’s best years are behind us. Americans are also far more pessimistic (44%) than optimistic (28%) when asked about what the US will be like 50 years from now. And this pessimism cuts across every demographic and is a shared national wound.

The pain is real — and, unlike last year when we documented how burnout was the energy-sucking vampire draining the American workforce, what we are witnessing now is something more extreme: complete mental, emotional and social collapse. People are not just tired. They are disconnected, despairing and done.

In fact, Gallup’s first-ever State of the World’s Emotional Health Report – Gallup, which surveyed 145,000 people across 144 countries, found in 2024 that 39% of adults worldwide reported feeling a lot of worry the previous day, 37% reported stress, 32% experienced physical pain, 26% felt sadness and 22% felt anger. All these figures are significantly higher than they were a few decades ago.

Inside the workplace, the numbers are just as alarming. Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace report states that for the first time since Gallup began tracking, more US workers are struggling than thriving. Employee engagement globally has fallen to 20% — its lowest level since 2020 — costing the world economy an estimated $10 trillion in lost productivity.

The “mic drop” moment: When companies answer the call, they win

However, herein lies the rub – the positive one — when companies genuinely invest in the well-being of their people as a core business strategy, they do extraordinarily well from a profit perspective, something that is integral to our philosophy at the Center for Social Capital, according to “Thriving Workplaces: How Employers Can Improve Productivity and Change Lives,” a report published by The McKinsey Health Institute in collaboration with the World Economic Forum. It concluded that investing in employee health could generate between $3.7 trillion and $11.7 trillion in global economic value — and boost global GDP by 4 to 12%.

Putting a powerful punctuation on all that is research, a portfolio of the 100 US companies with the highest employee well-being scores would have outperformed the S&P 500 by approximately 20%.

And in fact, that’s the pattern we launched our Center on — one we’ve been documenting for three years, sometimes even to our own surprise. We dug into it further in our latest feature at The Social Capital Insider, “The Well-Being Crisis Is a Business Emergency,” where we argue that business leaders have an incredible opportunity to lead a national recovery and resuscitation of the American Dream — and that those who invest genuinely in their people’s well-being, job security, and AI empowerment will build the most profitable enterprises of this generation.

And we were grateful to feature the insights of many leaders who are answering the call. Here are just a few of their exclusive insights.

At Delta Air Lines, CEO Ed Bastian has built an authentic and powerful wellness strategy that is both holistic and deeply practical. Delta has expanded its national network of pharmacies, launched a new nutrition program and made in-network care more accessible — all aided by an annual company-wide wellness survey that measures physical, emotional, social and financial health. One of the most tangible examples of that study’s efficacy was Delta’s Emergency Savings Program, which allows eligible employees to earn up to $1,000 from the company after completing financial education and contributing to an emergency savings account.

As Bastian puts it, “Our wellness strategy enables our people to be their best and enhances their sense of purpose, belonging and affinity by providing high-value health and wellness offerings.” And the philosophy behind it is simple: “At Delta, we do not only want our people to be well, but we want them to flourish. We know to take great care of our customers, our people must first take care of themselves.”

At Allianz Life, President and CEO Jasmine Jirele has elevated resilience from a corporate buzzword to a core life goal that the company can help its employees achieve. “For us,” explains Jirele, “this means supporting employees to balance workloads, take advantage of workplace flexibility… support a culture of listening, and encourage mental health support when employees need it.” So the company offers expanded hybrid flexibility around holidays and four fully remote weeks each year, trains managers to listen and support teams more effectively and helps employees handle unexpected events with greater confidence.

Their True Balance initiative integrates health, financial literacy, career growth and community into a single framework. Employees have free access to an on-site fitness and wellness center with group classes, cardio and strength equipment and personal trainers, as well as an on-site health clinic that provides comprehensive medical care at little to no cost — including services from a nurse practitioner and a mental health provider. And Jirele is particularly insistent that mental healthcare must be “accessible and affordable by providing it directly on campus.”

And finally, one of the greatest proofs is a company not only built on the very idea of mental well-being but also inspired by the complete loss of it.

In 2009, Jane McGonigal — a game designer with a Berkeley PhD — hit her head in her office and suffered a concussion that didn’t heal. For 30 days straight: nonstop headaches, nausea, vertigo, memory loss, mental fog. Her doctors told her the only treatment was simply to avoid any kind of mental stress or strain – in other words, abandon her career and her life. Instead, Jane McGonigal built SuperBetter, lying in bed, unable to read or work, trying to survive her own brain telling her there was no reason to live. She turned recovery into a game because a game was the only thing her damaged mind could handle.

Today, SuperBetter’s CEO, Keith Wakeman, is applying that same foundation to heal a different kind of injury — the one overwhelming millions of victims of modern life. “The human brain is under attack,” Wakeman writes. “The human brain is designed for a different time, and advances in digital technologies have made it relatively easy for others to exploit its vulnerabilities for their own benefit. As a result, employees feel increasingly unsettled, and struggle with stress, poor mental health, cognitive overload, difficult emotions and social disconnection.”

It’s almost a strange stroke of dumb luck that McGonigal’s brain injury after her physical trauma shares so much in common with the plight of the multitudes of victims of modern sensory and information overload who never hit their head at all, yet still their brains are turning against them, leaving them anxious, hopeless and terrified.

But Wakeman’s company carries the legacy of her antidote. “The good news is that employees and their families can be empowered with the ability to control their attention, use digital technology in ways that benefit them and defend against stress-based persuasion and cognitive exploitation.”

Together, these leaders are not just talking about wellness as a soft sideshow. They are building systems — financial, physical, emotional, social and technological — that treat well-being, stability, ownership and AI empowerment as the architecture of performance itself.

Opinions expressed by SmartBrief contributors are their own.

The project, first announced in August 2020, is intended to strengthen IndianOil’s petrochemical value chain at Paradip, in Odisha state, the company said in a statement on 28 July.

When complete, the complex will produce 800,000 tonnes/year of PX and 1.2 million tonnes/year of PTA, IndianOil previously said.

The company did not provide an updated commissioning schedule.

PX is the main feedstock for PTA, which is used largely in the production of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) resin and polyester fibers.

IndianOil also plans to invest about Rs43.82 billion in the Bhadrak Textile Park project through a joint venture with Indian PTA producer MCPI Private to support Odisha’s textile sector, the company said in the statement.

A further Rs10.6 billion is planned for a hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA)-based sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project through a joint venture with M11 Energy Transition.

The company did not disclose the proposed plant’s capacity or timeline.

IndianOil said it has invested about Rs433.5 billion at Paradip so far, including Rs345.6 billion in refinery units, Rs31.5 billion in its polypropylene (PP) plants and Rs56.54 billion in its monoethylene glycol (MEG) plant.

Its Paradip PP facility has a nameplate capacity of 680,000 tonnes/year, while the MEG plant has a capacity of 350,000 tonne/year, according to the ICIS Supply & Demand Database.

The movement underscores just how quickly Europe's renewable fuel sector has expanded.
Europe's biofuels market is becoming larger, more commercially significant, and increasingly interconnected: Stronger RED III implementation is translating into higher physical demand.
But the broader trend is becoming increasingly clear: Europe's renewable fuels sector is no longer being supported by policy alone.
text:
Europe's biofuels market entered 2026 expecting stronger demand. Six months later, those expectations have largely been confirmed.

Across the continent, consumption of renewable diesel (HVO) and biodiesel is accelerating under RED III, compliance obligations are increasing, and producers are operating in a market that is becoming both larger and more interconnected. Rather than struggling with a lack of demand, participants are increasingly focused on a different challenge: keeping pace with it.

That growing demand is now intersecting with higher oil prices, logistics constraints, planned refinery maintenance, and evolving global trade flows. These elements are creating a market that looks increasingly supportive of long-term investment across the biofuels value chain.

Demand Growth Is Becoming the Market's Defining Story

The strongest signal emerging from the first half of 2026 is simple. Europe's demand for renewable fuels continues to grow. Yet many market participants believe the full picture extends well beyond the official blending statistics.

For instance, Neste recently projected that RED III implementation could increase German HVO demand by approximately 1.5 million tons annually. Prima CarbonZero's own demand modeling suggests biodiesel and HVO demand across the EU could increase by roughly 2.5 million tons over the course of 2026.

Taken together, these indicators point toward a European market where demand growth is becoming increasingly structural rather than temporary.

Higher Energy Prices Are Reinforcing Biofuel Economics

Growing demand for renewable fuels is also coinciding with supportive conditions in conventional energy markets.

Following renewed uncertainty surrounding oil exports from the Persian Gulf, expectations for a near-term resolution to the US-Iran conflict have faded. As a result, crude oil and gasoil prices remain elevated.

For renewable diesel producers, that matters.

Higher gasoil prices raise the pricing floor for HVO, strengthening market economics even as production volumes increase. Rather than weighing on prices, stronger HVO sales throughout much of 2026 have generally been accompanied by firmer values. This reflects both stronger fossil fuel markets and tightening renewable fuel fundamentals.

Logistics Highlight the Value of Reliable Supply

Physical supply chains have become another important market signal.

An exceptionally hot European summer has drastically lowered the Rhine River water levels. This has reduced barge carrying capacity and increased inland freight costs throughout Germany.

The impact extends well beyond transportation for fuel blenders.

Reduced barge capacity limits the movement of renewable fuels to the locations where compliance obligations must be met. Consequently, logistics become an increasingly important component of market pricing. German traders have linked recent gains in the THG ticket market to these Rhine disruptions, illustrating how transportation bottlenecks can quickly influence compliance costs.

The situation also reinforces an important reality. As renewable fuel demand grows, dependable supply chains become just as valuable as production capacity itself.

High Utilization Leaves Little Room for Disruption

One of the clearest indicators of a healthy market is how fully production assets are being utilized.

Neste sold a record 623,000 tons of HVO in the European market during the second quarter, reflecting strong regional demand. Production temporarily exceeded sales, providing a modest inventory cushion. However, much of that surplus is expected to be absorbed during planned maintenance later this year.

Several planned maintenance outages could temporarily remove approximately 408,000 tons of production during the second half of the year. This represents roughly one-third of Neste's first-half European HVO sales.

Planned maintenance is a normal part of refinery operations. However, with demand continuing to strengthen, the market is entering the second half with relatively little excess capacity. The movement underscores just how quickly Europe's renewable fuel sector has expanded.

Global Trade Is Following the Strongest Markets

International trade is evolving alongside these stronger fundamentals as well.

Recent revisions to US import tariffs have improved the economics of exporting European biodiesel and waste-based feedstocks to the United States, where renewable diesel margins remain attractive. Europe has substantial grease-based biodiesel production capable of supplying the US market. Yet audit requirements for used cooking oil continue to limit the pace of some exports.

At the same time, US renewable diesel producers continue purchasing international waste feedstocks while exporting renewable diesel back into Europe. These dynamics highlight how increasingly connected global biofuel markets have become.

Chinese biodiesel also remains part of the European supply picture. But anti-dumping duties, reduced operating capacity, and the B7 blending limit continue to constrain significant growth in import volumes.

A Market That Continues to Mature

Viewed individually, higher oil prices, low Rhine water levels, refinery maintenance, or changing trade flows might appear to be short-term market events. Taken together, however, they tell a much bigger story.

Europe's biofuels market is becoming larger, more commercially significant, and increasingly interconnected:

Stronger RED III implementation is translating into higher physical demand.

Producers are operating at high utilization rates.

Global trade is increasingly flowing toward the regions with the strongest economics

Accordingly, infrastructure and logistics are becoming critical competitive advantages.

Short-term volatility will remain a defining feature of commodity markets. But the broader trend is becoming increasingly clear: Europe's renewable fuels sector is no longer being supported by policy alone. It is being reinforced by sustained demand growth, improving market economics, and growing confidence across the value chain.

For producers, feedstock suppliers, traders, investors, and fuel buyers alike, those are all signals of an industry entering its next phase of growth.

Public sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) are actively engaged in achieving these blending targets.

The information came in response to a question by Rajya Sabha member Smt. Phulo Devi Netam, who sought details on whether the Government had prepared a national roadmap for SAF blending in line with the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). She also asked about the volume of bio-jet fuel required to meet the 5% blending target by 2030 and measures to shield airlines from the higher cost of SAF.

In its reply, the Government said the PM JI-VAN Yojana, launched in 2019 and amended in 2024, provides financial assistance in the form of grants for setting up commercial and demonstration advanced biofuel plants, including Sustainable Aviation Fuel production facilities. The scheme is aimed at supporting the domestic production ecosystem needed to meet the country’s SAF blending targets.

text:
Grain trader Archer-Daniels-Midland said on Thursday it will invest in upgrades at four U.S. oilseed crushing facilities to expand North American processing capacity, as strong demand for renewable fuels drives growth in vegetable oil markets.

The company expects projects in Indiana’s Frankfort, Missouri’s Deerfield, Nebraska’s Lincoln and North Dakota’s Spiritwood to be completed between mid-2028 and early 2029, expanding processing capacity by about 700,000 metric tons annually.

U.S. demand for soybean oil and other vegetable oils has been rising as producers ramp up renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel capacity. In March, President Donald Trump’s administration had ordered refiners to blend a record amount of biofuels into gasoline and diesel in 2026 and 2027.

Soybean oil is a key feedstock for renewable fuels, alongside other sources such as used cooking oil and animal fats.

“Strong demand — supported by biofuels policy in the U.S. — is driving opportunities for farmers and the broader American agricultural sector,” said Gary McGuigan, president of ADM’s North America Ag Services and Oilseeds business.

ADM’s upgrades will include storage additions, equipment improvements and operational changes intended to increase throughput at the four facilities.

The expansion would create demand for more than 25 million additional bushels of U.S.-grown oilseeds annually, the company said.

ADM, which did not disclose financial details of the investments, said it is also evaluating similar upgrades at other North American crushing facilities.

In May, the company had raised its full-year profit forecast citing a strong oilseed processing outlook and clarity on U.S. biofuel blending mandates.

— Reporting by Pranav Mathur in Bengaluru

title: Lydian Raises $43 Million for Synthetic SAF - AVweb
description:
Boston-based Lydian announced a $43 million Series A funding round to support development of synthetic sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF).
The financing was led by Breakthrough Energy Ventures and will support the company’s PIVOT platform, which is designed to produce synthetic jet fuel from carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
Lydian says the system uses standardized, factory-built modules intended to reduce construction costs and respond to changes in renewable-electricity availability.
The company’s product differs from bio-based SAF because it is produced using captured carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
Its sustainability and emissions profile will depend on the sources of the hydrogen, electricity and carbon dioxide used during production.
text:
Boston-based Lydian announced a $43 million Series A funding round to support development of synthetic sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF). The financing was led by Breakthrough Energy Ventures and will support the company’s PIVOT platform, which is designed to produce synthetic jet fuel from carbon dioxide and hydrogen.

Lydian says the system uses standardized, factory-built modules intended to reduce construction costs and respond to changes in renewable-electricity availability. The company currently operates a pilot plant in Boston and plans to place a commercial demonstration facility into operation in 2028.

The company’s product differs from bio-based SAF because it is produced using captured carbon dioxide and hydrogen. Its sustainability and emissions profile will depend on the sources of the hydrogen, electricity and carbon dioxide used during production.

title: 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map - Sustainable Aviation
description:

To deliver the pathway set out in the 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map, it is imperative that we continue the strong partnership between industry and government.
The 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map provides our latest view, informed by experts drawn from across the UK Aviation industry, supplemented by independent experts.
2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map Summary Report Since becoming the first national aviation sector to commit to net zero by 2050, UK aviation has moved decisively from ambition to delivery.
This progress provides a strong foundation for the pathway set out in our 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map.
text:
Sustainable Aviation’s 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map presents an updated, ambitious plan based on several scenario-based pathways to deliver net zero carbon emissions through a combination of technological innovation, operational improvements, low carbon aviation fuel and Greenhouse Gas Removals.

The chart below is fully interactive to help you visualise these different potential futures dependent on policy support and investment achieved across government and industry.

Our full summary report can be read below or view the PDF available in the blue panel.

Note – This Road-Map chart shows rounded percentages – for complete figures please see the technical Road-Map. This Road-Map presents aviation’s purchase of emission allowances under the UK ETS Traded Emissions and is a ‘net contribution’ towards overall UK emission reductions. This recognises the price signal impacts of the UK ETS for airlines (as part of the sector’s total climate costs), and by calculating emission allowances purchased beyond aviation’s entitlement in the scheme, reflecting the sector’s contribution to wider decarbonisation efforts across all UK ETS covered sectors.

Foreword

by Neil Robinson, Chair of Sustainable Aviation

In 2020, the UK aviation industry was the first in the world to commit to net zero 2050. Since then, global airlines, and global governments through the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), have joined us to commit to the same goal.

UK aviation has moved on from goal setting and is now making tangible, positive progress. We’ve seen new, more efficient aircraft enter into service delivering an approximate 20% to 25% reduction in carbon emissions per passenger compared to the models they replace. Changes to aircraft operations and air traffic management have delivered more than 10 million tonnes of savings since 2008. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is now in regular use, with the UK’s SAF mandate exceeded in 2025, its first year of operation. Meanwhile new technologies such as hydrogen and zero emission flight continue to take shape.

As a result of the actions taken, UK aviation’s emissions are falling. Between 2005 and 2024, UK passenger numbers have increased by 28%, while aviation emissions have fallen by around 1% which would suggest that emissions per passenger have fallen by around 22%. When accounting for lifecycle emissions savings from SAF emissions have fallen by 2.5%. When including emissions covered by the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) as a ‘net contribution’ towards overall UK emission reductions delivered through compliance beyond the aviation share of emissions under the UK ETS, this would represent a reduction of 12.9%.

This progress provides a powerful foundation for the 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map. It shows that UK aviation can continue to grow, connect businesses, and take people on holiday, while staying firmly on the path to net zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Accelerating this positive trajectory is an incredible opportunity for the whole country. UK aviation is a cornerstone of our economy, contributing more than £100bn annually and supporting over 850,000 jobs across the UK. It connects friends and families, carries one third of all freight by value, and serves as a powerful engine for growth in other sectors.

As an industry, we are under no illusion that aviation is poised to become one of the biggest emitters of greenhouse gases. Climate change continues to be one of the challenges of our generation, and an existential risk to UK aviation. Yet again this year we’ve seen extreme weather conditions and new record temperatures set in May and June. This global warming makes the UK exceeding 40°C at least 20 times more likely than it was in the 1960s. The frequency of these heatwaves is putting unprecedented pressure on UK infrastructure, travel networks, and public health.

The UK is well placed to lead low carbon aviation, boasting world class aerospace and aviation companies, brilliant innovation capabilities, and a strong and growing policy framework. To deliver the pathway set out in the 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map, it is imperative that we continue the strong partnership between industry and government. To scale solutions, secure the UK’s global competitiveness, and keep flying affordable for everyone, we are calling on the Government to match our commitment with further decisive policy action.

With the right conditions in place, our sector will deliver net zero carbon emissions, playing a full part in meeting the Government’s commitment to decarbonise the UK economy. We will do so while continuing to drive economic growth, regional connectivity, and global competitiveness.

Executive Summary

UK aviation remains committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 while meeting growing demand to carry more passengers and freight.

This is an ambitious plan dependent on many variables, and requires a strong partnership between industry and government to ensure the right policy frameworks are in place. Throughout this transition, we must prioritise cost competitiveness and consumer affordability to avoid a customer rejection of net zero carbon emissions policies.

Tangible progress is already being made. Between 2005 and 2024 UK passenger numbers have increased by almost a third (28%) while aviation emissions have fallen by around 1%. Carbon emissions have fallen by 2.5% when accounting for lifecycle emission savings from Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF). When including emissions covered by the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) as a ‘net contribution’ towards overall UK emission reductions delivered through compliance beyond the aviation share of emissions under the UK ETS, this represents almost 13%.

This Road-Map shows how, with the right policy support, the industry can accommodate passenger growth of approximately 1.7 percent a year and reach net zero carbon emissions by 2050. The single largest contribution is from Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) – 31% by 2050. More efficient flight operations, more efficient aircraft currently in operation and next generation aircraft under development contribute another 24%. Emissions are also reduced by a further 15% due to slightly slower demand growth than otherwise would have occurred, due to increased ticket prices reflecting the cost of decarbonising. The remainder is expected to be absorbed by durable Greenhouse Gas Removals (GGRs) facilitated by existing or future compliance schemes such as the UK Emissions Trading Scheme or CORSIA.

The 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map provides our latest view, informed by experts drawn from across the UK Aviation industry, supplemented by independent experts. Whilst increased use of SAF remains the largest single contributor to emissions reduction, compared to our 2023 Road-Map there is an increased role for Greenhouse Gas Removals. This is primarily due to changes in their expected prices. The expected price of SAF has increased since 2023, while the expected price for GGRs has fallen. This illustrates that the decarbonisation pathways are likely to evolve over-time as technology and market conditions change.

There are challenges, both economic and political, to delivery. The technologies to decarbonise aviation exist, but they must be supported by the right policy frameworks, scaled at pace and at an acceptable cost, so that flying remains affordable for consumers. Whilst the UK aviation industry remains committed to delivering the Road-Map, we cannot do so alone and we look to the government to continue to build the necessary policy framework.

Our top priorities for the government

Maintain long-term funding for the Aerospace Technology Institute to sustain UK leadership in aircraft and engine efficiency development.

Continue cross-party and regulatory support to maintain momentum on the airspace modernisation programme.

Focus on keeping SAF costs as low as reasonably possible, by enabling access to global SAF supply and maximising SAF feedstock availability within robust sustainability guardrails.

Support the development of a UK SAF industry via first-of-a-kind pathfinder projects by finalising the Revenue Certainty Mechanism and accelerating planning approvals for SAF projects.

Prioritise the cost competitiveness of UK aviation by developing a robust commercial framework to scale domestic GGR supply at the lowest possible cost and ensuring access to verified international credits.

2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map Summary Report

Since becoming the first national aviation sector to commit to net zero by 2050, UK aviation has moved decisively from ambition to delivery. The focus is no longer whether decarbonisation can be achieved, but on how it can be delivered at pace, scale, and most affordably for passengers. There are many variables including some beyond the aviation industry’s control and, as such, the pathway is likely to continue to evolve over time. Delivering this transition will require effective action from the aviation industry, adjacent industries affected by Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and Greenhouse Gas Removals (GGRs), the UK and devolved governments, and international partners.

Aviation delivers enormous benefits. It connects friends and families, takes people on their holidays, enables businesses to grow, and carries one third of the world’s freight by value. It is one of the UK’s most important sectors, delivering growth and innovation directly, and enabling growth in other areas. The UK is a global leader in aviation, with world-class companies that export around the globe. The sector contributes around £100 billion a year to the UK economy. It supports more than 850,000 jobs and £20 billion in annual exports. In order to protect and grow these benefits, both now and in the future, we know that we have to decarbonise and address other environmental impacts such as non-carbon dioxide emissions and noise. This must be done in a way that supports UK aviation in what is a highly competitive global market.

UK aviation remains committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 while meeting growing demand to carry more passengers and freight.

Tangible progress is already being made. New aircraft entering service are more fuel-efficient than those they replace. The UK Sustainable Aviation Fuel Mandate was exceeded in its first year. Changes to airspace design are delivering carbon savings each and every day.

Between 2005 and 2024, UK passenger numbers have increased by almost a third (28%) while aviation carbon emissions have fallen by around 1% which would suggest that emissions per passenger have fallen by around 22%. Carbon emissions have fallen by 2.5% when accounting for lifecycle emission savings from SAF. When including emissions covered by the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) as a ‘net contribution’ towards overall UK emission reductions delivered through compliance beyond the aviation share of emissions under the UK ETS, this would represent a reduction almost reaching 13%.

This progress provides a strong foundation for the pathway set out in our 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map. It is set in the context of complex and rapidly shifting global market dynamics since our 2023 Road-Map. The UK aviation industry is navigating increasing costs that affect its competitiveness, ongoing geopolitical issues, challenges in scaling SAF and GGRs, legislative and regulatory developments, and the need to adjust delivery timelines for new commercial aircraft.

Reflecting these global dynamics, our modelling has been updated to include a scenario-based forecast. That will ensure this Road-Map remains realistic, credible, and resilient in the face of external volatility.

This Road-Map sets out how UK aviation can meet rising demand, drive economic growth and regional connectivity, and reach net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – provided the right policy framework is in place and technological advancement happens at the expected pace. Delivery now depends on partnership between industry and government to create cost-effective pathways, unlock investment, and maintain the UK’s competitiveness in a rapidly changing global aviation market.

Strategic pathways

Our Road-Map continues to draw on expertise from all corners of the UK aviation industry, including airlines, airports, aerospace manufacturers, the UK’s leading provider of air traffic control services – NATS, and wider supply chain and innovation organisations. It is based on a thorough review of the main opportunities to cut aviation carbon emissions, including operational efficiency, fleet renewal, airspace modernisation, SAF, effective carbon-based measures, and durable GGRs.

With the government focused on growth and consumers, the actions set out in our Road-Map show how the UK could accommodate significant growth in passenger kilometres of up to 54% whilst reducing net emissions from c.37 million tonnes of CO₂ per year down to net zero carbon emissions by 2050. It also shows how the aviation industry can drive this transition, helping to stimulate the growth of new technologies, creating thousands of new jobs, and providing economic advantage to the UK.

Demand and Growth

Government forecasts for aviation demand indicate continued growth to 2050. The Road-Map starts with the UK government’s unconstrained demand forecast, which estimates how many people would fly if there were no constraints, such as airport capacity, investment appetite, emissions trading, or Sustainable Aviation Fuel Mandates. This is a notional forecast, as many of these constraints exist now in the real world.

This Road-Map models the costs associated with the transition to net zero carbon emissions, including SAF uptake, carbon pricing, and GGRs. These costs are expected to moderately increase the price of flying and, as a result, temper demand (measured in Revenue Passenger Kilometres). Revenue Passenger Kilometres are still projected to grow significantly, by 54%, compared to 82% under unconstrained forecasts. This reduction in demand accounts for around 15% of total emission reductions by 2050, which equates to 10.3 million tonnes per year of carbon emission reductions by 2050, in our central scenario.

This Road-Map also models a high and a low scenario of 12% and 16% carbon reduction from cost-induced impacts respectively, which depends largely on SAF uptake and cost assumptions.

Including the cost-induced impact, passenger growth averages around 1.7% per year. This is closely aligned with long-term industry forecasts and reflects real-world constraints in the UK and internationally such as airport capacity, SAF mandates, and carbon compliance obligations. This Road-Map shows a pathway for the industry to accommodate this rate of passenger growth, deliver all the social and economic benefits that this brings, and reach net zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Operations and Air Traffic Management

Operational improvements across airlines, airports, and air traffic management provide near-term emission reductions. The airspace modernisation programme is already delivering carbon savings by replacing outdated routes and technologies with modern systems that enable more direct journeys, enhance capacity, and reduce fuel burn and carbon emissions, while supporting efforts to manage the impact of noise.

Much of the UK’s airspace was designed in the 1950s – a time with slower aircraft that relied on ground-based beacons. Today’s aircraft are faster, smarter, and far more advanced.

Recent UK changes to airspace are already enabling over 70,000 tonnes of CO₂ savings a year. NATS’s long-term plans are aligned with a contribution of around 1 million tonnes of carbon savings from all flights in domestic and oceanic airspace, equivalent to a 4.7% reduction in UK airspace emissions, based on 2019 traffic levels.

As passenger demand increases, the UK’s airspace modernisation strategy must proceed as quickly as possible to deliver carbon savings, improve noise management, create additional capacity, and build greater resilience into the system. The airspace change process set by the Civil Aviation Authority must become more efficient, transparent, and proportionate. Airspace modernisation is a critical enabler of aviation’s future – supporting growth, improving reliability and reducing emissions today while other decarbonisation solutions become available.

In this Road-Map, we expect continued progress from air traffic management, airline and airport operational initiatives to deliver around 4% of UK aviation decarbonisation by 2050 in our central scenario. We model between a low of 3% and a high of 6%, depending on the pace and completeness of implementation. This includes anticipated efficiency gains for departing flights across the wider international network, although some of these depend on changes outside the UK’s direct control.

To meet these ambitious targets, we urge the government to:

Continue cross-party and regulatory support to maintain momentum and move the airspace modernisation programme forward.

Ensure timely reform of the CAP1616 Airspace Change Process to reduce timescales and complexity, enabling changes to be delivered more efficiently while maintaining proportionate levels of scrutiny.

Deliver effective regulatory and legislative frameworks to support the implementation of the UK Airspace Design Service, ensuring it is empowered to enact airspace modernisation at the pace and scale required, including to support future airport expansion ambitions.

Provide adequate resourcing for the CAA and NATS to manage multiple airspace change programmes in parallel through the new UKADS service.

Aircraft efficiency and technological advancements

Fleet renewal remains a core pillar of the industry’s decarbonisation efforts. Aircraft entering service today are significantly more efficient than those they replace, delivering immediate and ongoing emissions savings.

The UK aviation industry’s rapid fleet renewal over the last few years has already delivered substantial carbon savings. Yet with around two-thirds of the UK narrowbody fleet still to be renewed, the approximate 20 to 25% efficiency improvement offered by each new aircraft still represents a strong decarbonisation opportunity.

This Road-Map predicts that aircraft already in service or under construction, classified as Generation 1 (G1), are expected to deliver around 10% of total decarbonisation by 2050. This is equivalent to approximately 7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions reductions a year by 2050.

We also estimate that next generation aircraft under development, classified as Generation 2 (G2), will deliver 25% efficiency improvements compared to the aircraft they replace, contributing a further 10% of total decarbonisation by 2050. That equates to another 6.9 million tonnes per year of carbon dioxide emissions reductions by 2050.

The entry into service timeline for hydrogen narrow body aircraft has been adjusted to reflect the complex engineering timelines required to mature novel technology, and to align with more conservative assessments of hydrogen production and infrastructure deployment schedules. Hydrogen is still expected to play a significant role in reducing aviation’s impact in the long-term, but its contribution up to 2050 is reduced, illustrating how decarbonisation pathways may adapt or evolve as technology readiness and market conditions change.

While narrow-body commercial hydrogen aircraft are now expected later than anticipated back in 2023, the overall decarbonisation trajectory remains broadly stable. Airlines are expected to deploy highly efficient aircraft using Sustainable Aviation Fuel and conventional fuels in the medium term.

To deliver this level of decarbonisation, the government needs to:

Maintain long-term funding for the Aerospace Technology Institute to sustain UK leadership in aircraft and engine efficiency development.

Support secure and skilled supply chains, including access to critical raw materials, so that costs and skills gaps are reduced, enabling high volumes of production of current and next-generation aircraft.

Fully recognise the strategic value of the aviation industry as key economic enabler and deliver a coherent plan supporting the industry to be globally competitive, including a focus on cumulative cost and regulatory burden.

Since we published our last Road-Map, airlines have invested significantly in upgrading their fleet. This progress, made between 2019 and 2024, has saved around 3.4 million tonnes a year in carbon emissions by 2024.

This Road-Map does not model a range for the impact of G1 aircraft technology on overall carbon emissions, because these efficiencies are largely fixed and already well known, but it does model a low and high scenario of 8% and 12% reduction in carbon emissions respectively for G2 aircraft.

To further support the industry in delivering the more ambitious levels of decarbonisation through the delivery of next generation aircraft, including hydrogen-powered and electric-powered aircraft over the long-term, the government should also consider:

Increasing the resources available to UK regulators to support the development of new standards and companies through the certification process.

Funding and establishing regulatory sandboxes to allow manufacturers, airports, and operators to trial advanced alternative propulsion configurations in controlled, real-world environments.

Supporting the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) in setting global efficiency standards for conventional aircraft and additional support for global schemes backing hydrogen.

If the critical enablers outlined above are pursued rigorously by both the UK government and international partners, next-generation aircraft could achieve up to a 30% efficiency gain, which could deliver carbon emission savings of approximately 12%. Conversely, a slower pace of implementation of the regulatory, investment, and international standards alignment proposals could significantly limit technical progress. Under these constrained conditions, next-generation aircraft might achieve a more modest 20% efficiency reduction, lowering their impact on mid-century decarbonisation to around 8%.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is central to aviation decarbonisation and remains one of the most effective ways to reduce carbon emissions. SAF is now used every day in flights across the UK, and the SAF mandate was exceeded in the first year of operation. The challenge now is to scale the supply of these proven technologies to meet growing demand.

The introduction of the UK SAF Mandate allows this 2026 Road-Map to model SAF deployment with greater clarity than previously. The UK SAF Mandate stipulates that 22% of aviation fuel is sustainable by 2040, which is materially lower than we modelled in previous Road-Maps.

Under the central scenario, we model SAF at 65% of total aviation fuel use by 2050, with an average lifecycle emissions reduction of around 80%, contributing around 31% of total decarbonisation in 2050. This is equivalent to approximately 21 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions reduced on a lifecycle basis.

This deliberately ambitious position is more than the government is currently adopting and reflects the industry’s commitment to decarbonise as much as possible within the sector, an expectation that, over time, a broader range of feedstocks will be available to meet the mandate, and that voluntary purchases of SAF may occur above the mandated level.

To deliver these reductions, the government needs to:

Focus on keeping SAF costs as low as reasonably possible by maintaining access to imports, scaling domestic SAF production, and avoiding buy-out penalties, to protect consumers and the competitiveness of UK airlines.

Maximise SAF feedstock availability within robust sustainability guardrails to support UK aviation competitiveness and avoid locked-in costs.

Finalise the secondary legislation relating to the SAF Bill to provide further clarity on the Revenue Certainty mechanism as soon as possible to support investor confidence in first-of-a-kind SAF projects in the UK, balance producer and consumer interests, and develop the UK SAF industry.

Continue to provide capital support for first-of-a-kind SAF plants though the Low Carbon Fuels Fund (LCFF) to support plants so that they can reach a final investment decision.

The ‘High’ SAF scenario sets out SAF usage at 70% of total fuel used, producing 33% of the overall total decarbonisation by 2050. This is equivalent to 22 million tonnes of carbon dioxide.

Further policy interventions could help to deliver this higher goal, such as:

Finding ways to expedite the planning process and reduce barriers, shortening both the time and expenditure required to go through planning approvals. The Lighthouse Green Fuels project is a great example of the types of initiatives that should be used.

UK leadership to support ICAO to encourage more global SAF production, including through bilateral agreements on SAF targets.

Ensure that carbon accounting rules take account of the role of imported SAF, including 3rd Generation Power-to-Liquid SAF.

Our ‘Low’ scenario shows that if SAF availability or affordability is lower, a fuel-share closer to 50% would deliver approximately 25% of total decarbonisation (17 million tonnes of CO2) with the remaining reductions met through other measures.

While SAF costs have increased relative to our 2023 assumptions, SAF is expected to grow as a global commodity, with domestic production enhancing energy security in volatile markets and delivering economic benefits for the UK alongside the emission reductions. Delivering the central scenario of 65% SAF by 2050 is ambitious and will require the aviation industry, the SAF industry, UK government and international partners to deliver at pace and scale. At present, near-term pressures, particularly around the supply of advanced SAF (i.e. 2nd and 3rd generation) need to be managed as this nascent industry begins to grow.

Greenhouse Gas Removals

Achieving the transition to net zero carbon emissions by 2050 requires reducing emissions at the source as much as possible while developing removal capabilities to manage the remaining emissions. UK aviation recognises that durable Greenhouse Gas Removals (GGRs) will play a vital role in balancing these residual emissions by mid-century, matching the broader cross-sector neutralisation strategies required for other challenging areas of the economy.

While SAF, operational improvements and more efficient aircraft deliver substantial emissions reductions, aviation is expected to remain a hard-to-abate sector. This Road-Map therefore assumes GGRs play an increasingly important role in addressing residual emissions that cannot be eliminated through in-sector measures alone. GGR deployment is assumed to scale progressively as technologies mature, costs fall and removals become integrated into carbon compliance markets. Achieving this outcome will require supportive policy frameworks, long-term investment certainty and the development of high-integrity removal markets in the UK and internationally.

In our central scenario, GGRs play a greater role than they did in the 2023 Road-Map. This is primarily due to lower SAF mandate levels, higher SAF costs, and more favourable cost projections for GGRs. Rather than functioning as direct decarbonisation measures, GGRs serve to physically balance the 19.5 million tonnes of residual carbon dioxide projected to remain annually by 2050, representing 29% of the total Road-Map architecture.

This remaining emissions framework is addressed through two distinct regulatory and market-based channels. In 2050:

Removals integrated within the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) are modelled to balance 5% of the sector baseline, which is equivalent to 3.6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, in line with emerging policy frameworks allowing verified removals to meet domestic compliance obligations.

A further 24% is addressed through future international and domestic obligations beyond CORSIA, equivalent to 15.9 million tonnes of carbon dioxide. This will require future international compliance pathways to transition away from carbon offsetting and move toward durable removals.

An independent report produced by Arup and CUR8 to inform this Road-Map forecasts that sufficient GGR capacity will be available to the aviation industry at a competitive cost. Scaling the GGR industry to meet this demand remains a key priority for the aviation sector. Through the Sustainable Aviation Advanced Market Signal framework, the industry is actively supporting both the demand and supply structures needed to commercialise and grow this market. However, the aviation industry cannot and should not shoulder the burden of scaling-up this industry alone.

Current market-based measures, including the UK ETS and CORSIA, will continue to support near-term aviation decarbonisation and are beginning the process of integrating GGRs into their architecture. The way GGRs are integrated into UK ETS, CORSIA, and post-CORSIA frameworks will be hugely important in decarbonising aviation.

To deliver these carbon savings, the government needs to:

Prioritise the cost competitiveness of UK aviation and develop a robust commercial framework including Contracts for Difference and capital support to scale domestic GGR supply at the lowest possible cost, while ensuring fair access to verified international credits.

Ensure policies affecting GGRs do not undermine SAF deployment, particularly in the critical near-term.

Evolve UK ETS so it fully recognises cost effective durable removals and continues pushing for durable removals to be integrated into the long-term compliance requirements for CORSIA – or any other international successor frameworks. This will ensure a level playing field for all airlines and keep the UK competitive.

Further government support should also consider:

Issuing Letters of Authorisation (LoAs) for a defined volume of UK-generated GGR credits under CORSIA, providing the corresponding adjustments required under Article 6.2 and enabling UK projects to access compliance markets. This would create a strong market signal for GGR deployment with minimal administrative burden and no direct public expenditure.

Implementing, in the long-term, tax deductibility frameworks for verified carbon removals to support the ongoing financial viability of aircraft operators.

Acting as an anchor buyer through direct government procurement to de-risk and accelerate this nascent industrial sector.

Conclusion

Aviation delivers enormous benefits to the UK, connecting people and businesses, delivering growth and innovation directly, and enabling growth in other areas.

Our Road-Map continues to present a robust, achievable, and credible plan for UK aviation to reach net zero carbon emissions by 2050. It sets out our assessment of the future trajectory, modelling a range of scenarios to reflect uncertainty and recognise that, over time, the decarbonisation pathways are likely to evolve as technology and market conditions mature.

The UK aviation industry remains committed to net zero carbon emissions by 2050, and to doing as much decarbonisation within the sector as it can – at the lowest cost possible to consumers – to preserve the benefits of flying for everyone.

There are challenges, both economic and political. Given the inherently global nature of aviation, the UK industry recognises that effective decarbonisation requires coordinated international action to maximise emissions reductions while balancing competitive advantage. The technologies to decarbonise aviation exist, but they must be supported by the right policy frameworks and grown at both pace and acceptable cost so that flying remains affordable for consumers. The industry is working hard and closely with government and other stakeholders to deliver this extremely worthwhile goal.

title: Shetland clean fuels hub making hydrogen and e-methanol gets cash boost
description:
A major clean fuels hub planned for Sullom Voe Terminal has received Scottish Government backing, supporting the development of low-carbon fuel production.
Veri Energy will receive almost £760,000 to fund the third phase of the project, which aims to begin producing hydrogen and e-methanol by 2030.
It is also intended to supply e-methanol to a proposed sustainable aviation fuel plant at the former Grangemouth refinery, strengthening Scotland’s emerging clean fuels supply chain.
Hydrogen and e-methanol are expected to play an increasingly important role in reducing emissions from sectors that are difficult to electrify, including aviation, shipping and heavy industry.
Developing domestic production will also improve energy security and support regional economic growth.

title: Can Syntholene make synthetic jet fuel cheaper than fossil fuels? - The Armchair Trader
description:

Syntholene is developing a new approach to producing synthetic hydrocarbon fuels using geothermal energy, captured carbon and highly efficient hydrogen production.
The company’s objective is ambitious: produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other synthetic fuels at costs that can eventually compete directly with conventional fossil fuels.

text:
Synthetic fuels have long been viewed as an expensive technology with enormous potential but little commercial viability. In the latest episode of the Investing, Markets & Money podcast, Syntholene CEO Dan Sutton explains why that perception may be about to change.

Syntholene is developing a new approach to producing synthetic hydrocarbon fuels using geothermal energy, captured carbon and highly efficient hydrogen production. The company’s objective is ambitious: produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other synthetic fuels at costs that can eventually compete directly with conventional fossil fuels.

Syntholene upsizes financing on back of investor demand

Syntholene achieves breakthrough in low cost geothermal hydrogen

Syntholene reaches key milestone in race to lower-cost synthetic aviation fuel

The discussion centres on one of the biggest challenges facing the global energy transition. Aviation remains one of the hardest sectors to decarbonise because jet fuel possesses an exceptionally high energy density that batteries cannot currently match. Sutton argues that synthetic kerosene offers a realistic pathway towards lower-emission aviation without requiring airlines to redesign aircraft or fuel infrastructure.

Demonstration plant in Ireland

A major milestone for Syntholene has been the successful commissioning of its demonstration plant in Iceland. Built alongside an existing geothermal power station, the facility began producing hydrogen just 69 days after permits were issued, demonstrating both rapid execution and the advantages of locating production where abundant geothermal resources already exist.

Rather than relying on intermittent renewable power sources such as wind and solar, Syntholene combines constant geothermal electricity with waste heat integration. According to Sutton, this significantly improves hydrogen production efficiency and could reduce production costs to below the much-discussed $2 per kilogram threshold widely regarded as a tipping point for the commercial hydrogen economy.

The conversation also explores why Iceland has become a strategic location for the business. Its plentiful geothermal resources, renewable electricity grid and streamlined permitting process provide an ideal environment for scaling industrial projects while avoiding many of the infrastructure constraints experienced elsewhere.

Wider applications

While sustainable aviation fuel is the immediate focus, the technology has much wider applications. Syntholene believes its process could ultimately produce synthetic diesel, gasoline, lubricants and other hydrocarbons with higher purity than conventional petroleum products.

For investors, the interview offers an early look at a company targeting a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars. Sutton argues that synthetic fuels represent one of the least understood opportunities within the wider clean energy transition, particularly as demand for global aviation continues to grow rapidly.

Looking ahead, the company plans to complete third-party validation of its demonstration plant before moving towards its first commercial-scale facility. If successful, Syntholene could become one of the companies helping to reshape the future of sustainable fuel production.

text:
ChemAnalyst Talks with Mr. Xiaofeng Ye, Vice President of Planetary Health Biosolutions APAC at Novonesis

Novonesis, a leading global biosolutions company created through the combination of Chr. Hansen and Novozymes, leverages microorganisms, enzymes, and biotechnology to develop sustainable solutions across more than 30 industries. Its biosolutions help improve resource efficiency, reduce carbon emissions, and enhance productivity in sectors including food, agriculture, energy, household care, and industrial manufacturing. ChemAnalyst spoke with Mr. Xiaofeng Ye, Vice President of Planetary Health Biosolutions APAC at Novonesis, about the company's strategy to accelerate biofuel adoption and industrial decarbonization across the Asia-Pacific region. Drawing on his extensive leadership experience, Mr. Ye highlighted Novonesis' partnership with Nhà Xanh Viet Nam to strengthen the country's bioethanol industry through advanced enzyme and yeast technologies that improve feedstock utilization, fermentation efficiency, and production economics. Looking ahead, he emphasized the company's commitment to advancing next-generation biofuels, supporting sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and low-carbon feedstocks, and fostering strategic collaborations that enable a more resilient, resource-efficient, and low-carbon energy future.

Complete Interview with Mr. Xiaofeng Ye

Q1: Please provide an overview of your professional journey in industrial biotechnology, biosolutions, and renewable fuels, and how these experiences have shaped your vision for Novonesis' role in advancing the global transition toward sustainable biofuels and industrial decarbonization.

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: I joined Novonesis in 2011 in the United States and have since held leadership roles across our global headquarters, North America, China, and Asia-Pacific, working with customers and partners across a wide range of markets and industries.

Today, as Vice President of Planetary Health Biosolutions for Novonesis Asia Pacific, I lead our work across areas including Bioenergy, agriculture, food, household care, and industrial applications. Across all these areas, our aim is simple: to help industries do more with less, using fewer resources, improving efficiency, and reducing their environmental impact.

My experience across business development, strategy, and innovation has strengthened my belief that biology has a big role to play in solving some of the world’s biggest challenges. I see biosolutions as a core part of building more resilient and sustainable industries for the future.

In renewable fuels, this means helping producers get more value from available resources, improve production efficiency, and develop locally produced, lower-carbon fuels that can support both energy security and economic growth.

Q2: Novonesis recently signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Nhà Xanh Viet Nam to support the country's bioethanol industry and E10 fuel rollout. What strategic objectives drove this partnership, and why is it a significant milestone for Vietnam's renewable energy transition?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: This partnership with Nhà Xanh represents an important step in supporting Vietnam’s transition towards more sustainable fuel options. With the country moving towards E10, it’s increasingly important to strengthen local bioethanol production and make it more efficient and cost-effective.

By producing more bioethanol from locally available resources, Vietnam can make better use of its agricultural resources, reduce its reliance on imported fossil fuels, and strengthen its energy security.

We are exploring ways to get more ethanol from the same amount of raw materials, lower production costs, and support the continued growth of Vietnam’s bioethanol industry by bringing our experience in corn- and cassava-based biofuel technology.

And the benefits go beyond energy. A stronger bioethanol sector can also create new opportunities for local farmers by increasing demand for crops such as cassava and corn, helping support a more sustainable and resilient agricultural sector.

Q3: Vietnam possesses abundant agricultural feedstocks such as cassava and corn. How will Novonesis' biosolutions improve feedstock utilization, strengthen domestic ethanol production, and enhance the country's long-term energy security?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: From the same amount of raw materials, our biosolutions help producers maximize the value of their cassava and corn by improving ethanol yields, increasing process efficiency, and making the fermentation process more robust and reliable. In addition to that, our partners in Vietnam can also leverage our expertise and learnings from other more mature bioethanol markets to further improve competitiveness.

Strong bioethanol industry could pave the way to more advanced renewable fuels such as sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) domestic production with bioethanol as feedstock in the future. Even co-products of the corn ethanol process, such as corn oil can be converted into biodiesel, renewable diesel, or even SAF today. These are relevant building blocks for strong energy security.

We believe that building a strong and competitive domestic bioethanol industry is key to Vietnam’s long-term energy security, especially as the country continues to be one of Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing economies with rapidly increasing energy demand.

Q4: Feedstock quality often fluctuates due to seasonal and agricultural conditions. How do Novonesis' biosolutions help producers maintain consistent fermentation performance, improve process stability, and maximize ethanol yields under varying feedstock conditions?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: With many variables out of producers’ control, uncertainty in this industry is a given. You have factors such as raw material shifts, raw material quality, and operating conditions all affecting performance. That’s why producers need solutions that can help maintain stable and efficient fermentation, even when conditions change.

We want to ensure that producers can get reliable, consistent results every time to reduce variability and operate with greater confidence. Our plant-tested, end-to-end solutions combined with experienced on-site technical support help producers achieve more consistent fermentation performance, improve process stability, and maximize ethanol yields.

Q4: Cost competitiveness remains one of the industry's biggest challenges. From a biotechnology perspective, what are the primary cost drivers in ethanol production, and how can enzyme innovation improve long-term production economics?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: Feedstock cost has always been the primary cost driver for bioethanol production. This is why making more ethanol from same amount of feedstock through both enzyme and yeast innovations is so important to improve competitiveness.

Another often overlooked factor is reliability of bioethanol fermentation. Fermentation can fail due to various factors which drives cost in the long run. It is also important to use solutions that can make the fermentation more robust and reduce risk of incomplete fermentation. Latest innovations of enzymes and yeast are designed to address this challenge.

Q5: While first-generation ethanol continues to dominate global production, interest in second-generation and waste-based biofuels is increasing. How is Novonesis preparing its biosolutions portfolio to support these next-generation renewable fuel technologies?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: We have invested in second-generation and waste-based biofuels for over 20 years, and we continue to drive innovation in this area.

Over that time, we have had a series of biotechnological breakthroughs, and we have been able to improve the economics of using biosolutions to produce second-generation biofuels. Novonesis is ready to support potential partners that are interested in exploring this segment.

Q6: Beyond the Vietnam collaboration, what are Novonesis' broader strategic priorities for supporting the growth of the biofuels industry across the Asia-Pacific region, and which markets offer the strongest long-term opportunities?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: We’re excited to see so many biofuels opportunities in most markets in Asia-Pacific, whether in bioethanol, biodiesel, or biogas.

Our priorities are quite simple. First, we want to offer the best biosolutions portfolio to support these different segments, leveraging our strong R&D capabilities. Second, we want to ensure a reliable supply of biosolutions to support biofuel production through our global production scale. And third, we want to build strong partnerships with biofuel producers across the region by providing experienced, on-the-ground technical support in key markets.

Q7: Governments worldwide are implementing higher ethanol blending mandates and stricter decarbonization targets. How do evolving regulatory frameworks influence investment decisions, technology adoption, and the commercialization of biotechnology-enabled renewable fuels?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: What we have seen in recent years is that policy is critical to accelerating the transition to renewable fuels. Faster regulatory approvals for bio-based alternatives, incentives that create a level playing field with fossil-based inputs, and investment frameworks aligned with the urgency of the energy transition are all essential to unlocking scale.

Mandates and decarbonization targets provide the market signals needed for companies to invest in new capacity, adopt new technologies, and accelerate innovation across the biofuels value chain.

Long-term success depends on creating the right conditions for continuous improvement, from increasing production efficiency to developing new solutions that can make renewable fuels more competitive and sustainable.

Q8: Renewable transportation fuels now include bioethanol, biodiesel, renewable diesel, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), biogas, and e-fuels. How do you see these fuel pathways complementing one another, and where does bioethanol maintain its strongest competitive advantage?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: The future energy system will require a range of solutions, as different sectors have different energy needs. I truly believe that biosolutions will play critical role in the overall global energy transition across many technologies.

In regions such as Southeast Asia, which have strong agricultural resources and growing energy demand, different renewable fuel pathways can complement each other, helping countries reduce emissions while strengthening energy resilience and creating value from local resources.

Looking ahead, one area with significant potential is the production of low-carbon-intensity (CI) sugars through biomass conversion.

Advancements in policies and demand for not just renewable fuels like sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and sustainable marine fuel (SMF), but also renewable chemicals like sustainable plastics and other biopolymers would help drive the demand for low CI sugars. Biomass conversion is steadily becoming more of a necessity, especially when other raw materials are becoming less available, such as used cooking oil for SAF.

Q9: Finally, what message would you like to share with ChemAnalyst's global audience regarding Novonesis' long-term vision for industrial biotechnology, biosolutions innovation, and its commitment to advancing renewable fuels, sustainable manufacturing, and the global energy transition?

Mr. Xiaofeng Ye: The world is changing fast, and industries and economies are already being reshaped by climate challenges, resource pressures, and unstable supply chains.
